# Statistical tables {#sec-appendix-tables}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Code in this appendix uses **R**.
:::

## Standard normal table {#sec-z-table}

Each entry in the table is the area under the standard normal curve **to
the left of** $z$, which is $P(Z < z)$, the shaded area in
@fig-z-table-area.

```{r}
#| label: fig-z-table-area
#| fig-cap: "The table gives the shaded area: the area under the standard normal curve to the left of $z$."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.4
library(ggplot2)
z0 <- 1.25
shade <- data.frame(x = seq(-3.5, z0, length.out = 200))
shade$y <- dnorm(shade$x)
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = shade, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, xlim = c(-3.5, 3.5), linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = z0, xend = z0, y = 0, yend = dnorm(z0),
           linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.3, y = 0.15, label = "P(Z < z)", size = 4.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, z0), labels = c("0", "z")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 13))
```

To find the area to the left of $z = 1.25$, go to the row for 1.2 and the
column for 0.05: the area is 0.8944. For a negative value such as
$z = -1.25$, use the row for $-1.2$ and the column for 0.05: the area is
0.1056.

For $z$ below $-3.49$, use 0.0001; for $z$ above 3.49, use 0.9999. The
areas there are smaller than 0.0001 and larger than 0.9999, respectively.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# rows are z to one decimal; columns add the second decimal (away from 0)
z_table <- function(rows) {
  cols <- seq(0, 0.09, by = 0.01)
  sgn <- ifelse(rows < 0 | (rows == 0 & 1 / rows < 0), -1, 1)
  areas <- outer(rows, cols, function(r, c) pnorm(r + sgn[match(r, rows)] * c))
  body <- matrix(sprintf("%.4f", areas), nrow = length(rows))
  labels <- sprintf("%.1f", abs(rows))
  labels <- ifelse(sgn < 0, paste0("−", labels), labels)
  out <- data.frame(z = paste0("**", labels, "**"), body)
  names(out) <- c("$z$", sprintf("%.2f", cols))
  out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-z-negative
#| tbl-cap: "Standard normal table: areas to the left of $z$, for negative $z$."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(z_table(c(-seq(3.4, 0.1, by = -0.1), -0)), align = "c")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-z-positive
#| tbl-cap: "Standard normal table: areas to the left of $z$, for positive $z$."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(z_table(seq(0, 3.4, by = 0.1)), align = "c")
```

## $t$ table {#sec-t-table}

Each entry in the table is a **critical value** $t$: the value with a given
area under the $t$ curve to its right, as in the left panel of
@fig-t-table-area. Because the $t$ curve is symmetric, the same value also
cuts off that area in each tail together, as in the right panel: the area
in two tails is twice the area in one tail.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-table-area
#| fig-cap: "Left: the area in one tail, to the right of $t$. Right: the area in two tails, outside $-t$ and $t$. The table gives $t$ for the areas at the top of each column."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.4
t0 <- 2
panels <- c("Area in one tail", "Area in two tails")
curve_t <- merge(data.frame(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 300)),
                 data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels)))
curve_t$y <- dt(curve_t$x, df = 10)
right <- data.frame(x = seq(t0, 4, length.out = 100))
right$y <- dt(right$x, df = 10)
tails <- rbind(cbind(right, panel = panels[1], side = "right"),
               cbind(right, panel = panels[2], side = "right"),
               transform(right, x = -x, panel = panels[2], side = "left"))
tails$panel <- factor(tails$panel, levels = panels)
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = tails, aes(x = x, y = y, group = side),
            fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = curve_t, aes(x = x, y = y), linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-t0, 0, t0), labels = c("−t", "0", "t")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

For example, with 10 degrees of freedom and an area of 0.025 in one tail
(0.05 in two tails), the critical value is 2.228. If the degrees of
freedom you need are not in the table, use the closest smaller value; this
gives a slightly wider, more cautious answer. The last row, for very many
degrees of freedom, gives the standard normal values.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t
#| tbl-cap: "Critical values of the $t$ distribution. Each column heading gives the area in one tail and the area in two tails."
#| echo: false
one_tail <- c(0.10, 0.05, 0.025, 0.01, 0.005)
t_df <- c(1:30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 1000, Inf)
t_body <- outer(t_df, one_tail, function(d, a) qt(a, d, lower.tail = FALSE))
t_tab <- data.frame(
  df = paste0("**", ifelse(is.finite(t_df), format(t_df, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "∞"), "**"),
  matrix(sprintf("%.3f", t_body), nrow = length(t_df)))
names(t_tab) <- c("Degrees of freedom",
                  paste0("One tail ", c("0.10", "0.05", "0.025", "0.01", "0.005"),
                         "<br>Two tails ", c("0.20", "0.10", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01")))
knitr::kable(t_tab, align = "c", escape = FALSE)
```

## Chi-square table {#sec-chisq-table}

Each entry in the table is a **critical value** $\chi^2$: the value with a
given area under the chi-square curve **to its right**, the shaded area in
@fig-chisq-table-area. Unlike the normal and $t$ curves, the chi-square curve
is not symmetric, so the left-hand columns (large areas to the right) give
values near the low end of the distribution, and the right-hand columns give
values far out in the right tail.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chisq-table-area
#| fig-cap: "The table gives the value $\\chi^2$ with the shaded area to its right."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.4
c0 <- 9.49
tail_c <- data.frame(x = seq(c0, 16, length.out = 100))
tail_c$y <- dchisq(tail_c$x, df = 4)
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = tail_c, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_function(fun = dchisq, args = list(df = 4), xlim = c(0, 16),
                linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 12.5, y = 0.05, label = "area to the right", size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, c0), labels = c("0", "χ²")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))
```

For example, with 4 degrees of freedom, the value with area 0.05 to its
right is 9.488. If the degrees of freedom you need are not in the table, use
the closest smaller value.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-chisq
#| tbl-cap: "Critical values of the chi-square distribution. Each column heading gives the area to the right of the critical value."
#| echo: false
right_area <- c(0.995, 0.99, 0.975, 0.95, 0.90, 0.10, 0.05, 0.025, 0.01, 0.005)
chi_df <- c(1:30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100)
chi_body <- outer(chi_df, right_area,
                  function(d, a) qchisq(a, d, lower.tail = FALSE))
# very small values need more than three decimal places
chi_txt <- ifelse(chi_body < 0.01,
                  formatC(signif(chi_body, 3), format = "fg"),
                  sprintf("%.3f", chi_body))
chi_tab <- data.frame(df = paste0("**", chi_df, "**"),
                      matrix(chi_txt, nrow = length(chi_df)))
names(chi_tab) <- c("Degrees of freedom", "0.995", "0.99", "0.975", "0.95", "0.90",
                    "0.10", "0.05", "0.025", "0.01", "0.005")
knitr::kable(chi_tab, align = "c")
```
